clinicalPearls: Tubulointerstitial diseases primarily affect the tubules and interstitium with relative sparing of the glomeruli and renal vessels, and are divided into acute and chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis (TIN) (Harrison 22e p.2437).

Classic allergic acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) presents with fever, rash, peripheral eosinophilia, and oliguric acute kidney injury occurring after 7-10 days of a beta-lactam (e.g., methicillin) - but this classic tetrad is the exception rather than the rule; patients are more often found incidentally to have a rising creatinine (Harrison 22e p.2438).
Acute TIN most often presents as acute kidney injury; today AIN is far more often an allergic reaction to a drug than a postinfectious phenomenon (Harrison 22e p.2437).

Urinalysis in allergic AIN shows pyuria with white blood cell casts and hematuria; white blood cell (leukocyte) casts are a characteristic finding of interstitial nephritis (Harrison 22e p.2438, p.2456).

The mainstay of treatment for drug-induced AIN is discontinuation of the offending agent, which often leads to reversal of kidney injury; glucocorticoids may accelerate recovery but are NOT required in most cases and are reserved for severe injury (Harrison 22e p.2438).

Chronic TIN is more indolent and manifests with disorders of tubular function: polyuria from impaired concentrating ability (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), Fanconi's syndrome from defective proximal reabsorption (glycosuria, phosphaturia, aminoaciduria, hypokalemia, and type II/proximal RTA from bicarbonaturia), or non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with hyperkalemia (type IV RTA) from impaired ammoniagenesis (Harrison 22e p.2437).

Proteinuria in chronic TIN is usually modest (rarely >2 g/d) from decreased tubular reabsorption of filtered proteins, but nephrotic-range albuminuria may occur when secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) develops (Harrison 22e p.2437).

Tubulointerstitial nephritis with uveitis (TINU) accounts for <5% of AIN, affects females 3x more than males, with median onset age 15 years; hallmark is painful anterior uveitis plus lymphocyte-predominant interstitial nephritis, with sterile pyuria, mild proteinuria, features of Fanconi's syndrome, and elevated ESR (Harrison 22e p.2439).

Sterile pyuria with elevated creatinine and features of Fanconi's syndrome should raise suspicion for TINU; ocular symptoms precede or accompany kidney disease in only one-third of cases (Harrison 22e p.2439).
Papillary necrosis is a key feature of analgesic nephropathy; a sloughed necrotic papilla can cause gross hematuria and ureteric colic from ureteral obstruction (Harrison 22e p.2442).
Renal ultrasound in reflux nephropathy characteristically shows asymmetric small kidneys with irregular outlines, thinned cortices, and regions of compensatory hypertrophy (Harrison 22e p.2441).
harrison.pathophysiology: A group of disorders that primarily affect the renal tubules and interstitium with relative sparing of the glomeruli and vessels, divided into acute and chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis (TIN) (Harrison 22e p.2437). Acute TIN causes AKI either via aggressive inflammatory infiltrates producing tissue edema, tubular cell injury, and compromised tubular flow, or via frank tubular obstruction by casts, cellular debris, or crystals; flank pain may arise from renal capsule distention (Harrison 22e p.2437). Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) is most commonly an allergic, immune-mediated drug reaction (antibiotics such as beta-lactams/sulfonamides/quinolones/vancomycin/rifampin, NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors, proton pump inhibitors, diuretics, anticonvulsants, allopurinol, immune checkpoint inhibitors), but may also be immune-mediated within autoimmune syndromes (Sjogren's, SLE, TINU, granulomatous/sarcoid, IgG4-related disease) or infection-associated (Harrison 22e p.2437-2438). Chronic TIN produces interstitial fibrosis with patchy mononuclear cell infiltration, widespread tubular atrophy, luminal dilation, and thickened tubular basement membranes, manifesting as tubular dysfunction (nephrogenic DI, Fanconi's syndrome, RTA) and progressive azotemia (Harrison 22e p.2437). Because the chronic histopathology is nonspecific, biopsy rarely yields a specific diagnosis, so diagnosis relies on history, drug/toxin exposure, associated symptoms, and imaging (Harrison 22e p.2437).
additionalDifferentials: Sjogren's syndrome with tubulointerstitial nephritis, distal RTA, and nephrogenic DI (Harrison 22e p.2438)
SLE with tubulointerstitial predominance and type IV RTA (Harrison 22e p.2439)
Light chain cast nephropathy / myeloma kidney (Harrison 22e p.2440)
Crystal deposition / obstructive tubulopathies (acute urate, acute phosphate, oxalate, drug crystals) (Harrison 22e p.2440)
Aristolochic acid nephropathy (Chinese herbal / Balkan endemic) (Harrison 22e p.2442)
infectionMimics: Acute bacterial pyelonephritis - infection-associated AIN should be distinguished from it; pyelonephritis does not generally cause AKI unless bilateral or causing septic shock (Harrison 22e p.2440)
Reflux nephropathy was previously mislabeled 'chronic pyelonephritis' because it was thought to result from recurrent childhood UTIs (Harrison 22e p.2441)
Infection-associated AIN, currently most often polyomavirus BK reactivation in kidney transplant recipients (Harrison 22e p.2440)
Granulomatous interstitial nephritis - tuberculosis must be ruled out before treatment, as it is a rare cause (Harrison 22e p.2439)
nonInfectiousMimics: Acute tubular necrosis and other causes of unexplained AKI (biopsy-proven AIN accounts for no more than ~15% of unexplained AKI, likely an underestimate) (Harrison 22e p.2437)
Primary glomerulonephritis causing secondary tubulointerstitial damage; in advanced disease the initial cause is often difficult to discern on biopsy (Harrison 22e p.2442)
Behcet's disease and sarcoidosis as alternative causes of uveitis when considering TINU (Harrison 22e p.2439)
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis - active sediment with leukocytes and cellular casts in acute TIN; pyuria with white blood cell casts and hematuria in allergic AIN; bland sediment in aristolochic acid nephropathy (Harrison 22e p.2437-2438, p.2442)
Peripheral blood eosinophil count - supports AIN but present in only a minority of patients (Harrison 22e p.2438)
Urinary eosinophils - NOT recommended; neither sensitive nor specific for AIN (Harrison 22e p.2438)
Serum creatinine and BUN to assess azotemia (Harrison 22e p.2437)
Anti-Ro (SS-A) and anti-La (SS-B) antibodies when Sjogren's syndrome suspected (Harrison 22e p.2438)
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis and immunofixation, plus serum/urine free light chains, when light chain cast nephropathy suspected (Harrison 22e p.2440)

Renal ultrasonography - 'medical renal disease' changes (increased echogenicity, loss of corticomedullary differentiation); asymmetric scarred kidneys in reflux nephropathy (Harrison 22e p.2437, p.2441)

Kidney biopsy - not usually required for AIN diagnosis but shows interstitial/tubular leukocyte infiltration including eosinophils; required (with other criteria) for aristolochic acid nephropathy (Harrison 22e p.2438, p.2442)
redFlags: Classic allergic AIN tetrad: fever, rash, peripheral eosinophilia, and oliguric AKI after a drug (Harrison 22e p.2438)
Particularly severe and rapid-onset AIN upon reintroduction of rifampin after a drug-free period (Harrison 22e p.2438)
Painful anterior uveitis (often bilateral, with blurred vision and photophobia) with sterile pyuria and AKI - suggests TINU (Harrison 22e p.2439)
Gross hematuria with ureteric colic from a sloughed necrotic papilla in analgesic or sickle cell nephropathy (Harrison 22e p.2442)
Triad of saturnine gout, hypertension, and impaired kidney function suggesting lead nephropathy (Harrison 22e p.2443)
Anemia disproportionately severe relative to kidney dysfunction in aristolochic acid nephropathy (with very high risk of upper urinary tract urothelial cancer) (Harrison 22e p.2442)
harrison.prognosis: In allergic/drug-induced AIN, discontinuation of the offending agent often reverses the kidney injury, though recovery may be incomplete depending on duration of exposure and degree of tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis (Harrison 22e p.2438). Granulomatous, idiopathic, TINU, and Sjogren's-related interstitial nephritis generally respond to glucocorticoids, especially when treated early before significant fibrosis, but may relapse and require maintenance immunosuppression (Harrison 22e p.2438-2439). Chronic TIN damage that has already occurred is impossible to reverse, but further deterioration may be slowed by treating glomerular hypertension (Harrison 22e p.2440). Reflux nephropathy affecting both kidneys often progresses inexorably to ESRD over years even without ongoing infection or reflux (Harrison 22e p.2441). Lithium-associated CKD is often irreversible and slowly progresses to ESRD even after lithium is stopped (Harrison 22e p.2443). AKI from acute hypercalcemia may be fully reversible, whereas chronic hypercalcemic kidney dysfunction may not improve even after correcting the calcium disorder (Harrison 22e p.2443).
pitfalls: The classic AIN tetrad (fever, rash, eosinophilia, oliguric AKI) is the exception rather than the rule; relying on it misses most cases (Harrison 22e p.2438).
NSAID-induced AIN often lacks fever, rash, and eosinophilia but presents with AKI and heavy proteinuria (Harrison 22e p.2438).
Urinary eosinophil testing is neither sensitive nor specific for AIN and is not recommended (Harrison 22e p.2438).
Absence of peripheral eosinophilia does not exclude AIN, as it is present in only a minority of patients (Harrison 22e p.2438).

A negative urine dipstick for protein with elevated total spot urine protein is highly suggestive of Bence-Jones protein (light chains), which dipsticks do not detect - missing myeloma kidney (Harrison 22e p.2440).
Reflux nephropathy may go unnoticed until adulthood and can be mistaken for 'chronic pyelonephritis'; a single affected kidney may be silent except for hypertension (Harrison 22e p.2441).
Because chronic TIN histopathology is nonspecific, biopsy rarely gives a specific diagnosis; over-reliance on biopsy without history/exposure analysis is a pitfall (Harrison 22e p.2437).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison classifies tubulointerstitial diseases into Acute Tubulointerstitial Disorders - acute interstitial nephritis (therapeutic agents/drugs, infection, autoimmune including TINU, Sjogren's, SLE, granulomatous, IgG4-related) and acute obstructive disorders (light chain cast nephropathy, acute phosphate nephropathy, acute urate nephropathy) - versus Chronic Tubulointerstitial Disorders (reflux nephropathy, sickle cell disease, chronic toxin/drug exposure such as analgesics, lithium, heavy metals, aristolochic acid, calcineurin inhibitors), metabolic disturbances (hypercalcemia/nephrocalcinosis, hyperuricemia, hypokalemia, hyperoxaluria, cystinosis), cystic/hereditary disorders, and miscellaneous causes (aging, chronic glomerulonephritis, obstruction, ischemia, radiation) (Harrison 22e p.2437).
management: Prompt withdrawal of the causative drug (implicated beta-lactam, sulfonamide, NSAID, proton pump inhibitor, allopurinol or immune checkpoint inhibitor) as the mainstay of drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis
A course of corticosteroids for severe or non-resolving acute interstitial nephritis to accelerate renal recovery
Treatment of the underlying cause in secondary disease, such as immunosuppression for sarcoidosis or Sjogren's and cessation of exposure in aristolochic-acid or heavy-metal nephropathy

Supportive correction of tubular dysfunction in chronic disease, with electrolyte and bicarbonate replacement for renal tubular acidosis and management of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and Fanconi features
Avoidance of further nephrotoxins and dose adjustment of renally cleared drugs
Monitoring of renal function and electrolytes, with dialysis support for severe acute kidney injury
Nephrology referral and, where the diagnosis is uncertain, renal biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and guide treatment
